name: Anti-looksmax / 'touch grass' critiques
lead: Critiques of looksmaxxing come from journalists, researchers, clinicians and others who argue the practice is harmful or misguided; a common informal version tells practitioners to 'touch grass', a phrase meaning go outside, used at people who seem absorbed in online content.[1][2] For people trying to improve their looks, the critiques are a map of the risks attached to particular methods and of the community's reputation, from injury-prone practices to ratings that can feed body dysmorphia.[1]

Wikipedia's looksmaxxing article records several lines of criticism: that the movement is judgmental, that mewing and 'bonesmashing' are regarded as misinformation by doctors and researchers, that it relies on anecdote and promotes male supremacy, and that it may channel young men toward incel views.[1] The same article carries a neutrality-dispute tag on its criticism section, and notes that some men report benefits such as peer approval or relationships.[1]
Some practitioners defend the practice; Wikipedia records men reporting benefits such as peer approval or relationships.[1]

paras: Writer Becca Rothfeld described the moral objections as numerous, severe and obvious in The New Yorker in 2026, pointing to the PSL scale's 'subhuman' category and slurs used by some practitioners.[1] Researchers Halpin and colleagues (2025, Sociology of Health & Illness) argue that looksmaxxing promotes a hegemonic masculine gaze on male bodies and reinforces male supremacy.[1]

Several authors call the PSL scale pseudoscientific, and researchers say evidence for mewing changing facial structure is lacking.[1] Facial surgeons warn that bonesmashing can cause fractures, misalignment, neurovascular injury and vision changes, and outlets including Vice, the Daily Dot and CBS Baltimore in 2023 labelled it misinformation, while Wikipedia calls it an inside joke that is rarely practiced.[1] Esquire's Bellot (2023) questioned whether TikTok tips can change jawlines.[1]

Riley Farrell (BBC, 2024), Simon Usborne (The Guardian, 2024) and Jamilla Rosdahl (The Conversation, 2024) report that communities that rate appearance can contribute to body dysmorphia and suicidal ideation. Rosdahl links its appeal to young men's sense of little control and argues it can pull them toward incel views, partly via TikTok algorithms.[1] Konig, Sidhu and Corpuz (2025) advise physicians to help patients separate safe beauty practices from harmful ones.[1]

Vanity Fair and Futurism criticised a five-drug 'pentastack' in 2026, and Wikipedia records public backlash after an April 2026 overdose by streamer Clavicular during a livestream.[1] Androgenic defended his own stack as less harmful than mixing alcohol and cocaine.[1]

Wikipedia's glossary describes 'touch grass' as believed to date from around 2015 and to have become popular again in 2020 and 2021, used to tell someone to go outside because they seem to have spent too long online.[2]
Farrell (2024) notes that some men report benefits such as getting a girlfriend or gaining peer approval, though the praise is usually mixed with critique.[1]

timeline.event: Approximate origin of the phrase 'touch grass'.[2]
BBC, The Guardian and The Conversation link rating communities to body dysmorphia and incel views.[1]
Halpin and colleagues publish a sociological critique in Sociology of Health & Illness.[1]
The New Yorker publishes Becca Rothfeld's critique.[1]

lore.intro: Critics and practitioners disagree about whether looksmaxxing is self-improvement or a harmful subculture.

claims.claim: Looksmaxxing rating culture harms mental health
claims.believers: Critics such as journalists at the BBC and The Guardian say rating communities can contribute to body dysmorphia.[1]
claims.experts: Academic commentators in 2025 describe the practice as resting on anecdote and a masculine gaze; no controlled study of looksmaxxing and mental health was found.[1]

claims.believers: Facial surgeons quoted in the press warn of fractures and nerve injury.[1]
claims.experts: Wikipedia says it is regarded as misinformation and an inside joke rarely practiced.[1]

claims.claim: Looksmaxxing is mostly grooming and fitness
claims.believers: Some men report benefits like peer approval or relationships, per Farrell (2024).[1]
claims.experts: Critics argue the movement's ideology and scales are harmful regardless.[1]

card.summary: The counter-discourse: journalists and researchers criticize looksmaxxing, while 'touch grass' is the informal version.

quick.overview:
This entry covers criticism of looksmaxxing, from academic and press critiques to the casual 'touch grass' jab.

Critics cite anecdote-based claims, injury risks and ties to incel ideology, while practitioners may see the criticism differently.
quick.mechanism: Critique appears in journalism, academic papers and online replies telling heavy users to go outside.
quick.risks: No direct risks; the topic concerns reported harms such as body dysmorphia and injuries from practices like bonesmashing.

chain: Critics identify harmful or unsupported practices
Readers weigh risks and claims before trying methods
Practitioners adjust how they pursue looks improvement
angle.text: The critiques document where looksmaxxing methods carry injury risks or rest on anecdote, and where rating culture affects wellbeing, which informs how people choose what to try.
